title: If and then
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedTenses: condizionale presente — five verbs only (vorrei, potrei, dovrei, sarebbe, verrei)
congiuntivo imperfetto — one cell (avessi), in one counterfactual frame

rules.text: SE PLUS THE PRESENT IS ENGLISH'S "IF" AND NOTHING ELSE. Se piove, resto a casa lines up word for word with "If it rains, I'm staying home", and a learner braced after L3-M3 for another mood will invent a trap that is not there. The one real difference is small and worth saying: the second half is far more often a plain present in Italian than English would allow — Se domani ho tempo, andiamo al mare, where English wants "we'll go". Both are correct Italian; the present is what is said.

THE CONDIZIONALE IS A TENSE, AND THIS COURSE HAS BEEN USING IT SINCE L1-M3. vorrei was shipped as a frozen politeness at L1-M3, and L2-M1 shipped two more the same way — potrebbe and potresti. None of the three was ever explained, because a tense had not been opened. They are one tense: vorrei, potrei, dovrei, sarebbe, verrei all end the same way, and the three words already in your mouth are the proof that the endings are learnable.

THE ENDINGS, ONCE: io is -ei, tu is -esti, lui and lei are -ebbe. vorrei / vorresti / vorrebbe, potrei / potresti / potrebbe, dovrei / dovresti / dovrebbe. This module opens the tense on five verbs and no more — volere, potere, dovere, essere and venire — because five is what the sentences need. The rest of the verbs are L4's, and the endings above are what they will take.

ONE COUNTERFACTUAL FRAME, AND IT IS BUILT FROM TWO PIECES: se avessi (a past form the course does not otherwise own) and then the condizionale. Se avessi tempo, verrei — I don't have the time, so I am not coming. Both halves move, and neither one is a plain present. The paradigm behind avessi is L4-M3's; this module owns the one cell and the one shape of sentence it builds.

WHAT YOU WILL ACTUALLY HEAR IS OFTEN SIMPLER, AND THAT IS NOT A MISTAKE TO HIDE. Spoken Italian very often puts the plain imperfetto in BOTH halves — Se avevo tempo, venivo — where the textbook wants se avessi tempo, verrei. It is ordinary, unremarkable speech, not slang and not an error to correct in someone. Write the first; recognise the second when it reaches you, because a course that denies what a learner hears stops being believed.

ADVICE IS THE CONDIZIONALE, NOT AN ORDER. Dovresti parlare con il capo is what a friend says; Devi parlare con il capo is what a boss says, and English's "you should" hides the difference because it is one word either way. Potresti, sarebbe meglio and io al posto tuo do the same softening job, and none of them needs a mood or a new tense.

sentences.cue: If it rains, I'm staying home

words.note: The bare if, kept free by L3-M3's anche se being one whole key. It behaves exactly as English's "if" — here in a condition, and in L3-M5 in a reported yes/no question.
A plain -are verb. The noun resto is the change a shop hands back, and the two are told apart by what stands in front of them.

sentences.trap: There is no trap here and saying so is the lesson. After L3-M3 a learner expects every conjunction to bend the verb; se plus the present does not, and neither does the half that follows it.
sentences.sound: se PYO-ve, RES-to a KA-za. piove is two syllables, PYO-ve, with the i swallowed into the p.

variations.display: Se piove, non esco
variations.cue: If it rains, I'm not going out
variations.changed: the negative in the second half

variations.display: Se piove, resto in ufficio
variations.cue: If it rains, I'll stay at the office

variations.display: Se non piove, andiamo al mare
variations.cue: If it doesn't rain, we're going to the sea
variations.changed: the condition negated, and a noi verb

mistake.display: Se piove, io resto a casa mia
mistake.why: The pronoun and the possessive are both spare here: Se piove, resto a casa.

sentences.usage: The most-said conditional there is, and it costs nothing new.
sentences.mnemonic: se + present = if + present. No trap.

sentences.display: Se domani ho tempo, andiamo al mare
sentences.cue: If I have time tomorrow, we'll go to the sea
sentences.literal: If tomorrow I-have time, we-go to-the sea

words.note: One word for both: ho tempo is "I have time" and che tempo fa is "what's the weather". Context separates them and nothing else does.

sentences.trap: English cannot say "if I have time tomorrow, we go to the sea" — it needs "we'll go". Italian says the present and means the future, and this is the one place se differs from "if" at all.
sentences.sound: se do-MA-nee o TEM-po. The h of ho is silent, so ho tempo runs together as o-TEM-po.

variations.display: Se domani ho tempo, vado al cinema
variations.cue: If I have time tomorrow, I'll go to the cinema

variations.display: Se ho tempo, andiamo al mare domani
variations.cue: If I have time, we'll go to the sea tomorrow

variations.display: Se non ho tempo, resto a casa
variations.cue: If I don't have time, I'll stay home

mistake.display: Se domani ho il tempo, andiamo al mare
mistake.why: The phrase takes no article: Se domani ho tempo, andiamo al mare.

sentences.usage: Half-promising a day out, which is what most conditionals are for.
sentences.mnemonic: Italian says the present and means tomorrow.

sentences.display: Vorrei tornare presto, ma potrei restare
sentences.cue: I'd like to go back early, but I could stay
sentences.literal: I-would-want to-return early, but I-could to-stay

words.note: The io cell of the same tense as L2-M1's potresti and potrebbe. Same verb, same endings, one row apart: potrei, potresti, potrebbe.

sentences.trap: vorrei has been in your mouth since L1-M3 and was never explained, because there was no tense to explain it with. There is now: vorrei is to volere exactly what potrei is to potere, and neither is a polite word — both are one cell of the condizionale.
sentences.sound: vor-RE-ee ma po-TRE-ee. Both end on a stressed è plus a light i, and the double r of vorrei is held.

variations.display: Vorrei tornare presto
variations.cue: I'd like to go back early
variations.changed: the frozen half on its own

variations.display: Potrei restare a casa
variations.cue: I could stay at home
variations.changed: the new cell on its own

variations.display: Vorrei restare, ma devo tornare
variations.cue: I'd like to stay, but I have to go back
variations.changed: the plain present in the second half

mistake.display: Vorrei di tornare presto, ma potrei di restare
mistake.why: A conditional takes the bare infinitive, exactly as a present modal does: Vorrei tornare presto, ma potrei restare.

sentences.usage: Saying what you want and what you might do instead, in one line.
sentences.mnemonic: vorrei and potrei are the same tense wearing different verbs.

sentences.display: Dovrei studiare, ma sono molto stanco
sentences.cue: I should study, but I'm very tired
sentences.literal: I-should to-study, but I-am very tired

words.note: The condizionale of L3-M2's devo, and a whole world softer. devo studiare is a duty; dovrei studiare is a duty you are admitting you will not do.

sentences.trap: English's "should" and "have to" are two different words, so the pair reads as two verbs. In Italian it is ONE verb in two tenses — devo and dovrei — and the softening is entirely in the ending.
sentences.sound: do-VRE-ee stoo-DYA-re. dovrei loses the vowel devo has: it is do-VREI, never do-ve-REI.

variations.display: Dovrei studiare, ma non ho tempo
variations.cue: I should study, but I don't have time

variations.display: Dovrei lavorare, ma sono stanco
variations.cue: I should work, but I'm tired

variations.display: Non dovrei uscire stasera
variations.cue: I shouldn't go out tonight

mistake.display: Devo studiare, ma sono molto stanco
mistake.why: That is a duty, not an admission. The soft one is the conditional: Dovrei studiare, ma sono molto stanco.

sentences.usage: The sentence everybody says to themselves in the evening.
sentences.mnemonic: devo is a duty. dovrei is a duty you are dodging.

sentences.display: Dovresti parlare con il capo domani
sentences.cue: You should talk to the boss tomorrow
sentences.literal: You-should to-talk with the boss tomorrow

words.note: The tu cell, with the same -esti ending as L2-M1's potresti. It is advice between equals; devi in the same seat is an instruction.

sentences.trap: English says "you should" to a friend and to an employee alike. Italian does not: dovresti is a suggestion you may decline and devi is not, and choosing devi where a friend expected dovresti lands as an order.
sentences.sound: do-VRES-tee. The stress is on the VRES, and the final i is short and clear.

variations.display: Potresti parlare con il capo domani?
variations.cue: Could you talk to the boss tomorrow?
variations.changed: L2-M1's cell, doing the same softening

variations.display: Dovresti tornare a casa presto
variations.cue: You should go back home early

variations.display: Non dovresti lavorare il sabato
variations.cue: You shouldn't work on Saturdays

mistake.display: Devi parlare con il capo domani
mistake.why: That is an order. Advice to a friend is the conditional: Dovresti parlare con il capo domani.

sentences.usage: The everyday shape of advice, and the one an English speaker gets wrong by being too direct.

sentences.display: Io al posto tuo, vorrei restare a casa
sentences.cue: If I were you, I'd want to stay home
sentences.literal: I at-the place your, I-would-want to-stay at home

words.cue: if I were you · in your place
words.note: ONE key of three words: "in your place". The possessive comes AFTER the noun here and takes no article of its own — never al tuo posto in this phrase.

sentences.trap: English builds this out of a past tense — "if I were you" — and Italian builds it out of a noun. There is no verb inside al posto tuo at all, so nothing in it has to be conjugated; the conditional lands on the advice that follows.
sentences.sound: ee-o al POS-to TOO-o. tuo is two syllables, TOO-o, and the io in front is fully sounded.

variations.display: Io al posto tuo, vorrei tornare a casa
variations.cue: If I were you, I'd want to go back home

variations.display: Al posto tuo, vorrei parlare con il capo
variations.cue: In your place, I'd want to talk to the boss

variations.display: Io al posto tuo, potrei restare qui
variations.cue: If I were you, I could stay here

mistake.display: Io al tuo posto, vorrei restare a casa
mistake.why: The phrase is fixed with the possessive last: Io al posto tuo, vorrei restare a casa.

sentences.usage: Advice given by standing in the other person's shoes rather than by telling them what to do.
sentences.mnemonic: al posto tuo — the possessive goes last.

sentences.display: Sarebbe meglio tornare a casa presto
sentences.cue: It would be better to go back home early
sentences.literal: It-would-be better to-return at home early

words.note: The lui/lei cell of essere in the condizionale, with the same -ebbe ending as potrebbe. Sarebbe meglio is the most-used piece of advice in the language.

sentences.trap: There is no it in the Italian. sarebbe carries the subject in its ending, so Sarebbe meglio is a whole sentence where English needs three words in front of "better" before it can start.
sentences.sound: sa-REB-be MEL-yo. The double b is held, and the gli of meglio is the lli of million.

variations.display: Sarebbe meglio parlare con il capo
variations.cue: It would be better to talk to the boss

variations.display: Sarebbe bello tornare a Roma
variations.cue: It would be lovely to go back to Rome

variations.display: Non sarebbe meglio restare a casa?
variations.cue: Wouldn't it be better to stay home?

mistake.display: Sarebbe meglio di tornare a casa presto
mistake.why: No preposition before the infinitive: Sarebbe meglio tornare a casa presto.

sentences.usage: Advice with nobody named in it, which is the least confrontational shape there is.
sentences.mnemonic: Sarebbe meglio — two words, whole advice.

sentences.display: Se avessi tempo, verrei anche io
sentences.cue: If I had time, I'd come too
sentences.literal: If I-had time, I-would-come also I

words.note: A past form that lives only after se, in the frame below. It says the opposite is true: se avessi tempo means the time is exactly what I do not have.
The io conditional of venire, irregular in its stem and regular in its ending — verrei, verresti, verrebbe. The double r is held.

sentences.trap: Both halves move, and an English speaker moves only one. "If I had time, I would come" puts the change in the second half; Italian changes se avessi as well, and se ho tempo, verrei is neither the real condition nor the unreal one.
sentences.sound: se a-VES-see TEM-po, ver-RE-ee. Both double consonants are held, and avessi ends on a clear ee.

variations.display: Se avessi tempo, verrei domani
variations.cue: If I had time, I'd come tomorrow

variations.display: Se avessi i soldi, verrei anche io
variations.cue: If I had the money, I'd come too

variations.display: Se avessi tempo, verrei al mare
variations.cue: If I had time, I'd come to the sea

mistake.display: Se ho tempo, verrei anche io
mistake.why: An unreal condition moves both halves: Se avessi tempo, verrei anche io.

sentences.usage: Turning an invitation down while making clear you wanted to accept. Said out loud, though, Italians very often use the plain imperfetto in both halves — Se avevo tempo, venivo — and it is ordinary speech, not a slip: write the frame above, and expect to hear that one.
sentences.mnemonic: Unreal: se avessi … verrei. Both halves move.

sentences.display: Se ho i soldi, vado a Roma domani
sentences.cue: If I have the money, I'll go to Rome tomorrow
sentences.literal: If I-have the money, I-go to Rome tomorrow

words.note: Plural in Italian where English is singular: i soldi, never il soldo in this sense. Everything around it agrees in the plural too.

sentences.trap: soldi is plural and "money" is not, so English pulls a singular verb and a singular article after it. Ho i soldi, and the article is there in Italian where English has none.
sentences.sound: se o ee SOL-dee. ho i runs as one long o-ee, because the h is silent.

variations.display: Se ho i soldi, vado al mare
variations.cue: If I have the money, I'll go to the sea

variations.display: Se non ho i soldi, resto a casa
variations.cue: If I don't have the money, I'll stay home

variations.display: Se hai i soldi, andiamo a Roma
variations.cue: If you have the money, we'll go to Rome

mistake.display: Se ho soldo, vado a Roma domani
mistake.why: Money is plural and takes its article: Se ho i soldi, vado a Roma domani.

sentences.usage: The real condition against S08's unreal one — this one might actually happen.
sentences.mnemonic: i soldi — plural, with its article.

sentences.display: Se hai un problema, dovresti chiamare subito
sentences.cue: If you have a problem, you should call right away
sentences.literal: If you-have a problem, you-should to-call immediately

words.note: Stressed on the FIRST syllable, SOO-bee-to, and it has nothing to do with English "subtle" or with anything sudden. It means now, not soon.

sentences.trap: The two halves of this module meet here and neither one changes the other: se plus a plain present on the left, the conditional of advice on the right. A condition does not make advice unreal, and advice does not bend the condition.
sentences.sound: SOO-bee-to. First syllable stressed; a learner who says soo-BEE-to will be understood and heard as a foreigner.

variations.display: Se hai un problema, dovresti chiamare
variations.cue: If you have a problem, you should call

variations.display: Dovresti chiamare subito il capo
variations.cue: You should call the boss right away
variations.changed: who to call, and no condition

variations.display: Se hai un problema, potresti chiamare subito
variations.cue: If you have a problem, you could call right away
variations.changed: the softer of the two conditionals

mistake.display: Se hai un problema, devi chiamare subito
mistake.why: Advice, not an order: Se hai un problema, dovresti chiamare subito.

sentences.usage: The whole module in one line — a real condition and a piece of advice.
